Detailed method

The calculator opens at 4 balls of 250 g, with 65% hydration, 2.8% salt, and 0.2% yeast. That little yeast is there for a long, cold rise, not a fast afternoon dough. These times assume you only change the flour amount and keep the percentages the same. Still judge the dough by how it looks and feels.

  1. Mix Stir the flour, water, and yeast until no dry flour remains, then work in the salt. At the opening recipe the dough is soft but not soupy. Aim for about 24°C (75°F).
  2. Rest Cover the bowl and leave it for 20 minutes. The 65% dough smooths out and stops tearing when you fold it.
  3. Bulk Keep it covered at about 24°C (75°F) for 1 hour. Give it one stretch-and-fold halfway through. It should look a little puffier, not doubled. With only 0.2% yeast, most of the rise happens later in the cold.
  4. Ball Divide the dough into the number of balls on the calculator. The page opens at 4 balls of 250 g. Tighten each one so the skin is smooth, then set them in a covered tray with a little space between them.
  5. Cold ferment Refrigerate the balls at about 4°C (39°F) for 16 to 24 hours. They should spread slightly and smell mildly yeasty, not sharp.
  6. Warm and stretch Take the balls out 60 to 90 minutes before baking. Stretch each one by hand on a floured peel: leave a thick rim and a thin center. A rolling pin presses the rim flat.
  7. Bake Heat a stone or steel at 250°C (480°F), or as hot as the oven will go, for 45 minutes. Slide the pizza on and bake 6 to 8 minutes, until the rim is spotted and the center is set. A very hot oven around 430°C (800°F) needs only 60 to 90 seconds.
  8. Rest Set the pizza on a rack for 2 minutes before you cut it, so the center stops flowing.
